message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is not legal advice; if you have a specific dispute, consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear).
• Landlord must provide a written itemized statement of deductions. | Keep a copy of the lease, move‑in photos, and receipts for repairs. Ask for a written receipt when you pay the deposit. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Texas Property Code §92.001 requires landlords to keep premises in a safe, sanitary condition and to repair major defects.
• Tenants may withhold rent only if the landlord fails to make necessary repairs after notice. | Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) and keep a copy. If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may consider withholding rent or filing a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office. | | **Notice Requirements** | • **Month‑to‑month**: 30‑day written notice to terminate.
• **Fixed‑term lease**: 30‑day notice before the lease ends.
• **Eviction**: Landlord must give a written notice of the reason and a 3‑day (or 30‑day for non‑payment) notice before filing an unlawful detainer action. | Use certified mail or a reliable delivery service to prove notice was received. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on how much a landlord can raise rent, but they must give **30 days’ written notice** for a month‑to‑month lease or **30 days’ notice** before the lease renewal. | Review your lease for any “rent increase” clauses. If the landlord raises rent without proper notice, you may refuse to pay the new amount until the notice period expires. | | **Discrimination** | Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or handicap. | Keep records of any discriminatory remarks or actions. File a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24–48 hours) before entering the unit, except in emergencies. | Ask for a written notice schedule if you suspect frequent unannounced visits. | | **Lease Termination & Eviction** | • Landlord can evict for non‑payment of rent, violation of lease terms, or criminal activity.
• Tenant can terminate for “constructive eviction” if the landlord fails to maintain habitability. | Document all communications. If you receive an eviction notice, you have 30 days to respond or contest it in court. | | **Legal Remedies** | • Small claims court (up to $20,000) for disputes over deposits, unpaid rent, or damages.
• You can file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office or the local housing authority. | Keep all receipts, photographs, and written correspondence. These will be crucial evidence in court or mediation. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand the terms, deposit limits, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos of the unit at move‑in/move‑out, written notices, repair requests. 3. **Know the Notice Rules** – 30‑day notice for most actions; 3‑day notice for non‑payment before eviction. 4. **Keep Records of Rent Payments** – Receipts, bank statements, or online payment confirmations. 5. **Know When to Seek Legal Help** – If the landlord violates habitability standards, refuses to return a deposit without justification, or engages in discriminatory practices. ### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | File complaints against landlords, get legal guidance. | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Fair Housing complaints, educational materials. | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal clinics, mediation services. | | **Texas Small Claims Court** | Resolve disputes over deposits, unpaid rent, or damages. | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, a fair security‑deposit process, proper notice before entry or eviction, and protection from discrimination. Keep detailed records, communicate in writing, and know the statutory notice periods. If you encounter a problem, use the resources above to protect your rights.
